The river runs along a long valley between the Serra do Mar and the Serra da Mantiqueira, linking the states of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and reaches the Atlantic after about 1,100 km.
ne-rv-1159116437.w: Two mountain ranges frame a wide valley; the river runs down its middle, lined with towns, a highway and farmland.
f: The basilica at Aparecida is one of the largest Catholic churches in the world.
Much of Rio de Janeiro's water supply is pumped from the Paraíba do Sul.
In the 19th century its valley was Brazil's great coffee-growing region.

q.q: What did fishermen pull from the Paraíba do Sul in 1717?
q.a: A statue of the Virgin Mary

Q18278.t: The river that gave a country its name
Q18278.s: A whole country took its name from this river: Uruguay lies on its eastern bank. Here, far upstream, the Uruguay is a green-brown river winding through rolling hills of forest and farmland, with Brazil on one bank and Argentina on the other. A little upstream it tumbles over the Moconá Falls, which run lengthwise along the river rather than across it.
Q18278.w: A deep green valley between rolling hills, with forest and patchwork farmland on both banks of the river.
f: Uruguay's official name means 'Eastern Republic of the Uruguay' – the land east of this river.
It runs about 1,800 km and, with the Paraná, forms the Río de la Plata.
Its name is often translated from Guaraní as 'river of the painted birds'.

q.q: Which river joins the Uruguay to form the Río de la Plata?

Q21806688.t: So muddy it keeps losing its own way
Q21806688.s: The Pilcomayo carries so much silt down from the Bolivian Andes that it keeps choking its own bed. Here it leaves the foothills and enters the flat Gran Chaco, where three countries meet on its banks. Further on, much of its water spills into shifting marshes, and its channel moves from year to year.
Q21806688.w: A pale, silty river with a wide sandy bed across flat, olive-green Chaco scrub, with dry channels branching off.
f: Its sediment load is among the highest of any river in the world.
It rises in the Andes of Bolivia, near Potosí.
For much of its course it forms the border between Argentina and Paraguay.

q.q: On which river do Argentina, Bolivia and Paraguay meet?

Q2635327.t: Dark water through the heart of bonobo country
Q2635327.s: Endless rainforest, broken only by the dark, twisting line of the Tshuapa: this is the heart of the Congo Basin. The river winds west for about 1,000 km, joining other streams to reach the Congo near Mbandaka, a city on the equator. Its basin lies south of the Congo River, the only region in the world where wild bonobos live.
Q2635327.w: A narrow, dark river twisting through unbroken, deep-green rainforest, its banks almost hidden by the canopy.
f: The province of Tshuapa, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is named after the river.
Its water reaches the Congo by way of the Busira and the Ruki.
Salonga National Park, Africa's largest tropical rainforest reserve, lies to its south-west.

q.q: Which great ape lives wild only south of the Congo River?

Q273456.t: Highland gorges down to a jade desert lake
Q273456.s: The Omo never reaches the sea. It drops from the Ethiopian highlands through deep, forested gorges, then winds south across hot lowlands to end in Lake Turkana, a jade-green lake in the desert. Its lower valley has yielded some of the oldest known fossils of our own species.
Q273456.w: A brown river twisting through a deep, wooded gorge, with green highland ridges rising on either side.
f: The Omo supplies around 90% of the water flowing into Lake Turkana.
The Lower Valley of the Omo has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1980.
Fossils found at Omo Kibish in 1967 are among the oldest known remains of Homo sapiens.

q.q: Which lake does the Omo River flow into?

Q2001150.t: Savanna water bound for Lake Chad
Q2001150.s: The Ouham rises in the north-west of the Central African Republic and flows north through wooded savanna, a dark thread of gallery forest in the grass. Across the border in Chad it becomes the Bahr Sara and joins the Chari, whose water ends in Lake Chad. In the rainy season it swells and spreads over its floodplain.
Q2001150.w: Rolling, tree-dotted savanna with scattered villages; the river shows as a dark line of gallery forest.
f: The Ouham is one of the main headwaters of the Chari, the river that feeds Lake Chad.
A prefecture of the Central African Republic is named after it.
Bossangoa, the main town on its banks, lies not far upstream of here.

q.q: What is the Ouham called after it crosses into Chad?

Q2591927.t: Under the forest canopy, bound for the Congo
Q2591927.s: The Kadéï begins in the forests of eastern Cameroon and flows east and south-east into the Central African Republic, a narrow, dark river under a green canopy. At Nola it meets the Mambéré, and together they form the Sangha, which flows on south through vast rainforest to join the Congo River.
Q2591927.w: Dense green forest with only a few clearings and roads, and a narrow dark river snaking through it.
f: The Sangha, which it helps to form, crosses the Sangha Trinational, a UNESCO site shared by three countries.
The forests of its basin shelter forest elephants and western lowland gorillas.
Nola, where it meets the Mambéré, is a small river port in the Central African Republic.

q.q: The Kadéï and the Mambéré join to form which river?

Q746779.t: The wild line between Tanzania and Mozambique
Q746779.s: For most of its roughly 800 km the Ruvuma is the border between Tanzania and Mozambique, running east through wild miombo woodland to the Indian Ocean. Its wide, sandy bed is braided with channels and green islands. To the south lies the Niassa Reserve, one of Africa's largest protected wildernesses.
Q746779.w: A wide, sandy, braided river with green islands, crossing flat woodland with few roads or villages.
f: The first bridge across it, the Unity Bridge, opened in 2010.
David Livingstone tried to use the Ruvuma as a route inland in 1861–62.
The Niassa Reserve covers some 42,000 km².

q.q: Which two countries does the Ruvuma separate?

Q14299.t: Castles, a world-dividing treaty and port wine
Q14299.s: On the vast, wheat-coloured plateau of Castile, the Duero is a green line of poplars and fields. Near here, at Tordesillas, Spain and Portugal signed the 1494 treaty that divided newly explored lands overseas between them. Downstream the river becomes the Douro and carves a deep valley of terraced port vineyards on its way to Porto.
Q14299.w: A vast, flat plateau of golden and brown farmland, crossed by a thin green line of trees and fields.
f: Simancas castle, on its banks, has held Spain's royal archives since the 16th century.
The Alto Douro wine region in Portugal became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2001.
For about 100 km it forms the Spanish–Portuguese border in a deep canyon, the Arribes.

q.q: What did Spain and Portugal divide at Tordesillas in 1494?

Q8510.t: Afghanistan's longest river, fading into the desert
Q8510.s: Afghanistan's longest river begins in the Hindu Kush west of Kabul and runs about 1,150 km south-west, a green ribbon of fields across ever-drier land. Here it skirts the red dunes of the Registan desert, then turns north into the Sistan basin, where it spreads into shallow lakes and marshes that shrink and swell with the seasons.
Q8510.w: A thin green ribbon of fields along a river, red sand dunes on one side and bare gravel desert on the other.
f: The Helmand has no outlet to the sea; it ends in the Hamun lakes of the Sistan basin.
Its name comes from its ancient Avestan name, Haetumant.
The Registan desert beside it is a sea of reddish sand dunes.

q.q: Where does the Helmand River end?

Q206850.t: Rust-red with silt, running straight for Hanoi
Q206850.s: The river's name says it: laden with red-brown silt, it looks like a stripe of rust in a deep green valley. It rises in Yunnan, where it is called the Yuan, and runs south-east in a remarkably straight line along a great fault before crossing into Vietnam at Lao Cai. Downstream it passes Hanoi and builds the fertile Red River Delta.
Q206850.w: A reddish-brown river running in a straight, deep valley between steep green mountain ranges, heading south-east.
f: Upstream in Honghe, the Hani have carved spectacular rice terraces into the mountains, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The Red River is about 1,150 km long.
Hanoi's name means 'inside the river', for its place in a bend of the Red River.

q.q: Which capital city stands on the Red River?

Q132726.t: The river of the Taj Mahal, winding past Agra
Q132726.s: Just upstream, the Taj Mahal stands on a bend of the Yamuna at Agra. From cruise height look instead for the river itself, a pale, sandy ribbon looping across the flat plain, and to the south the badlands of the Chambal, a maze of eroded ravines. Downstream the Yamuna meets the Ganges at Prayagraj, one of Hinduism's holiest places.
Q132726.w: A pale, sandy river looping across a flat, farmed plain, with a maze of deeply eroded ravines to the south.
f: The Yamuna rises at the Yamunotri glacier in the Himalaya.
At about 1,375 km it is the longest tributary of the Ganges.
Delhi, India's capital, grew up on its banks.

q.q: At which city does the Yamuna meet the Ganges?

Q234004.t: Flowing west while India's great rivers go east
Q234004.s: Most of India's great rivers flow east to the Bay of Bengal; the Narmada goes west. It runs about 1,300 km through a long rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges to the Arabian Sea. Here, at Hoshangabad, now renamed Narmadapuram, it is a broad river lined with bathing ghats. Pilgrims walk its whole length, down one bank and back up the other.
Q234004.w: A broad river running east–west in a long, straight valley, wooded hills to the south and a town on its south bank.
f: Near Jabalpur the river cuts through a gorge of white marble cliffs at Bhedaghat.
The Narmada is traditionally seen as the dividing line between northern and southern India.
The Sardar Sarovar dam on its lower course is one of the largest in India.

q.q: Which sea does the Narmada flow into?

Q1075393.t: Stone watchtowers above a roaring gorge
Q1075393.s: Western Sichuan's mountains squeeze the Dadu into narrow, roaring gorges, walled by slopes that rise thousands of metres. Around Danba, Tibetan villages and ancient stone watchtowers cling to terraces above the river. Further south it passes beneath Gongga Shan, 7,556 m high, before meeting the Min at Leshan, beside the Giant Buddha.
Q1075393.w: A thin river deep in steep, forested gorges, with snow-capped peaks rising to the south-west.
f: The Leshan Giant Buddha, carved in the 8th century where the Dadu meets the Min, is 71 m tall.
The iron-chain bridge at Luding has spanned the Dadu since 1706.
The Dadu is about 1,060 km long.

q.q: Which giant statue stands where the Dadu meets the Min?

Q841359.t: The world's longest river on an island
Q841359.s: No river on any island on Earth is longer than the Kapuas: about 1,140 km from the mountains of central Borneo to the sea. Here at Sintang it swings in wide, brown loops through forest and plantation. Upstream it feeds the Danau Sentarum lakes, which fill in the wet season and shrink to muddy channels in the dry.
Q841359.w: A wide brown river looping through a patchwork of dark forest and pale plantations, with a town at a river junction.
f: Pontianak, at its mouth, sits almost exactly on the equator.
The Danau Sentarum lakes can rise and fall by many metres between seasons.
The Kapuas is the longest river in Indonesia.

q.q: What record does the Kapuas hold?

Q216875.t: Spanned by the world's highest railway bridge
Q216875.s: The Chenab gathers glacier water high in the Himalaya and races through deep, steep-sided gorges on its way to the plains of Punjab. Near here its canyon is spanned by a steel arch railway bridge about 359 m above the water, the highest railway bridge in the world. The river is born where two streams meet, the Chandra and the Bhaga.
Q216875.w: A blue-green river winding in a deep, steep gorge between forested ridges, with snowy peaks further north.
f: Its upper course, where the Chandra and Bhaga meet, is also called the Chandrabhaga.
Downstream it takes in the Jhelum and the Ravi, then joins the Sutlej on the way to the Indus.
It is one of the five rivers that give Punjab its name.

q.q: Which two streams form the Chenab?

Q26390.t: A surprise pocket of forest in Chukotka's tundra
Q26390.s: Chukotka is mostly bare tundra and mountain, but along the middle Anadyr, around the village of Markovo, poplars, willows and larches grow in a surprising pocket of forest. The river winds east for about 1,150 km across lake-strewn lowlands to the Bering Sea. In 1649 Semyon Dezhnev's men built a winter fort on its banks.
Q26390.w: A broad, braided river through flat, pale tundra full of lakes, with darker patches of riverside woodland.
f: The Anadyr is the largest river of Chukotka.
Dezhnev reached the Anadyr after being shipwrecked on his voyage round Asia's eastern tip in 1648.
The town of Anadyr, at its mouth, is the easternmost town in Russia.

q.q: Whose men founded a fort on the Anadyr in 1649?

Q216188.t: Coal country, taiga and ancient rock art
Q216188.s: The Tom crosses the Kuznetsk Basin, one of Russia's great coal fields, where huge grey open-pit mines are cut into the green hills. Rising in the Kuznetsk Alatau, it runs about 830 km north past Novokuznetsk, Kemerovo and Tomsk to the Ob. On riverside rocks near Kemerovo, ancient people carved elk, bears and birds.
Q216188.w: A green river valley of forest and fields; further south, grey terraced coal pits stand out in the hills.
f: The rock carvings of Tomskaya Pisanitsa, near Kemerovo, are several thousand years old.
Tomsk, founded in 1604, is one of the oldest cities in Siberia and is named after the river.
The Tom joins the Ob a little downstream of Tomsk.

q.q: Which Siberian city takes its name from the Tom?

Q1468689.t: Central America's longest river, deep in the jungle
Q1468689.s: The Coco is usually counted as the longest river lying entirely within Central America, about 700 km from the hills of Honduras and Nicaragua to the Caribbean. For much of its course it forms the border between the two countries, winding through dense forest. The Miskito people call it the Wangki; it reaches the sea at Cape Gracias a Dios.
Q1468689.w: Dense, dark-green forest with few clearings, split by a brown river that doubles as a border.
f: Columbus named Cape Gracias a Dios, 'thanks be to God', in 1502 after escaping a storm there.
The Bosawás Biosphere Reserve, one of Central America's largest forests, lies along its Nicaraguan side.
It is also known as the Segovia River.

q.q: What do the Miskito people call the Coco River?

Q196183.s: Fields of corn and soybeans stretch in a perfect grid across the flat Midwest, and the Wabash cuts through them in a wooded, winding valley. From a dam near Huntington it flows unimpeded for about 660 km to the Ohio, one of the longest free-flowing stretches of river east of the Mississippi. It is Indiana's state river, and the state song is about it.
Q196183.w: A narrow wooded valley cutting diagonally through a flat grid of square fields.
f: 'On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away' has been Indiana's state song since 1913.
Along its lower course it forms the border between Indiana and Illinois.
The Wabash is about 810 km long.

q.q: Which state's official song is about the Wabash?

Q607546.t: Plunging into a gorge, reversed by the tides
Q607546.s: At Grand Falls the Saint John drops about 23 m into a deep, narrow gorge. Upstream it forms part of the border between Maine and New Brunswick, and potato fields spread around it in neat stripes. At its mouth the Bay of Fundy's huge tides push back against the river, reversing the rapids at the famous Reversing Falls.
Q607546.w: Long, striped fields and woods on both sides of the river, and a small town beside a narrow gorge.
f: Samuel de Champlain named the river after reaching its mouth on St John the Baptist's day in 1604.
Its Wolastoqey name, Wolastoq, means 'beautiful river'.
The Saint John is about 670 km long.

q.q: What happens at the Reversing Falls at the river's mouth?

Q134350.t: Straightened by hand, still scarred with old loops
Q134350.s: The Great Hungarian Plain is flat as a table, and across it the Tisza winds between dikes, surrounded by the ghostly curves of former meanders. In the 19th century engineers cut through more than a hundred of its loops, shortening the river by hundreds of kilometres to tame its floods. It is the longest tributary of the Danube, about 960 km.
Q134350.w: Curving oxbow lakes and old meander scars all over a flat plain, with the river held between dikes.
f: Each June, swarms of long-tailed mayflies hatch over the river in what Hungarians call the 'Tisza blooming'.
Lake Tisza, a reservoir upstream, has become a large wetland reserve for birds.
The river rises in the Carpathians and touches five countries on its way to the Danube.

q.q: Which river is the Tisza the longest tributary of?

Q838143.t: Born in the world's first protected wilderness
Q838143.s: The Gila rises in the mountains of New Mexico, in the Gila Wilderness, which in 1924 became the first area anywhere officially protected as wilderness. From there it winds west across Arizona, a thin green line of cottonwoods through brown desert ranges. Much of its water is used before it reaches the Colorado at Yuma, and long stretches lie dry.
Q838143.w: A thin green ribbon of trees and fields winding through dry, brown mountains and desert basins.
f: The Gila monster, a venomous lizard, is named after the river's basin.
The Gila is about 1,040 km long.
The conservationist Aldo Leopold campaigned for its headwaters to be protected.

q.q: What was set aside in the Gila's headwaters in 1924?

Q173017.s: Rudyard Kipling called it 'the great grey-green, greasy Limpopo River, all set about with fever-trees', and the description still fits: a wide, sandy riverbed, often nearly dry, lined with dark green trees in pale bush. Here it forms the border between South Africa and Zimbabwe. It runs about 1,750 km to the Indian Ocean in Mozambique.
Q173017.w: A wide, pale sandy riverbed with a dark green fringe of trees, winding east through dry, grey-brown bush.
f: Mapungubwe, upstream where the Shashe joins, was the heart of a powerful kingdom around 1200 and is now a UNESCO site.
Downstream at Pafuri, on the edge of Kruger National Park, three countries meet on its banks.
In the dry season long stretches of its bed hold no flowing water at all.

q.q: Which writer called the Limpopo 'great grey-green, greasy'?

Q920267.t: Larch, tundra and ice on the Taymyr lowlands
Q920267.s: Far above the Arctic Circle, the Kheta winds east across the lowlands of Taymyr, where scattered larches give way to open tundra and countless lakes. It lies frozen for most of the year and passes only a few small settlements. Where it meets the Kotuy, the river takes a new name, the Khatanga, and flows on to the Laptev Sea.
Q920267.w: Flat, pale tundra and sparse larch woodland dotted with countless lakes, the river curling east through it.
f: The Kheta is about 600 km long.
Dolgan reindeer herders and fishermen live in the villages along its banks.
Ary-Mas, on a nearby tributary of the Khatanga, is often called the northernmost forest in the world.

q.q: The Kheta and which river form the Khatanga?

Q903306.t: Texas's 'river of the arms of God'
Q903306.s: Spanish explorers named it Río de los Brazos de Dios, 'the river of the arms of God', and the name was later shortened. Here, south of Fort Worth, it winds through rolling ranch country and wooded hills, dammed into long, branching lakes. The Brazos crosses Texas from the High Plains to the Gulf of Mexico, one of the longest rivers in the state.
Q903306.w: Rolling ranchland with a wooded river valley that widens into long, branching reservoirs.
f: Dinosaur tracks can be seen in the bed of the Paluxy, a Brazos tributary, at Glen Rose.
Texas declared its independence in 1836 at Washington-on-the-Brazos.
Stephen F. Austin's colony of American settlers grew up along its lower course in the 1820s.

q.q: What does the Brazos's full Spanish name mean?
q.a: River of the arms of God

Q237901.t: The 'wild horse without reins' of the Taklamakan
Q237901.s: The Tarim runs along the northern edge of the Taklamakan, one of the world's great sand deserts, and its shifting channels have earned it a Chinese nickname: 'the wild horse without reins'. Along its banks grows a belt of desert poplars, gold in autumn, that marks the river as a dark band across the sand. It has no outlet to the sea.
Q237901.w: A braided river with a dark belt of poplar woods along it, the pale dunes of the Taklamakan to the south.
f: Its riverside poplar forests are among the largest of their kind in the world.
Lop Nur, the lake it once fed at its far end, has dried up.
Counted from the Yarkand's source, the Tarim is over 2,000 km long, China's longest inland river.

q.q: Which desert lies along the Tarim's southern bank?

Q385342.t: Four names along its course, and rarely much water
Q385342.s: This long river system changes its name as it goes: Desaguadero, then Salado, then Chadileuvú and Curacó, as it drains the dry foothills of western Argentina south towards the Río Colorado. So much of its water irrigates the vineyards and orchards of Mendoza and San Juan that its lower course across La Pampa is often thin or dry, with scattered marshes.
Q385342.w: A faint, winding river line with salt flats and marshes across flat, dry, grey-green scrubland.
f: Desaguadero means 'drain' or 'outlet' in Spanish.
Upstream it flows through the Guanacache lagoons, a protected wetland.
In wet years its water can reach the Río Colorado, far to the south.

q.q: What does the Spanish name Desaguadero mean?

Q138491.t: Somalia's lifeline, winding to the Indian Ocean
Q138491.s: In the dry bush of southern Somalia, the Jubba is a green lifeline: a winding brown river edged by fields of maize, sesame and bananas. It forms on the Ethiopian border, where the Genale and the Dawa meet, and flows about 1,000 km south to the Indian Ocean near Kismayo. Unlike its neighbour the Shabelle, it usually reaches the sea.
Q138491.w: Flat, dry, reddish bushland crossed by a brown river with a narrow green band of fields and trees.
f: Together with the Shabelle, the Jubba waters most of Somalia's farmland.
It reaches the sea just south of the equator.
Its flow rises sharply when the rains fall on the Ethiopian highlands.

q.q: Near which port does the Jubba reach the Indian Ocean?

Q210326.t: The river Harbin carves its ice palaces from
Q210326.s: Every winter the Songhua freezes thick, and Harbin cuts huge blocks of its ice to build the glowing palaces of its famous ice festival. The river rises at Heaven Lake on Changbai Mountain and runs about 1,900 km across the plains of north-east China to the Amur. Here, east of Harbin, it winds in wide loops through a flat patchwork of fields.
Q210326.w: A broad, looping river with sandbars and green islands across a flat grid of farmland, white and frozen in winter.
f: The Songhua is the largest tributary of the Amur.
Upstream at Jilin, mist from the unfrozen river coats the trees in dazzling winter rime.
Harbin's ice festival dates back to 1963.

q.q: Which city builds ice palaces from the frozen Songhua?

Q1321316.t: Long, inland, and often lost in a swamp
Q1321316.s: The Lachlan is one of Australia's longest rivers, yet it often fails to arrive anywhere: in dry years it runs out into the Great Cumbung Swamp before reaching the Murrumbidgee. It rises in the Great Dividing Range and winds west across flat, dusty plains of wheat and red earth, lined with river red gums.
Q1321316.w: A thin, winding line of dark river red gums across flat plains of red earth and pale wheat fields.
f: Surveyor George Evans named it in 1815 after Lachlan Macquarie, governor of New South Wales.
Its water reaches the Murrumbidgee, and then the Murray, mainly in wetter years.
The Lachlan is about 1,450 km long.

q.q: Which governor is the Lachlan River named after?

Q621609.t: Ending in marshes alive with waterbirds
Q621609.s: Downstream of Warren the Macquarie spreads out into the Macquarie Marshes, a maze of reed beds and red gum swamps where huge numbers of waterbirds breed after a flood. It rises in the Great Dividing Range near Bathurst and flows north-west for about 950 km across the plains. In wet years it continues on to join the Barwon.
Q621609.w: A thin line of dark river red gums across a flat patchwork of fields, spreading north into green marshes.
f: Bathurst, on its upper course, founded in 1815, is Australia's oldest inland city.
Like the Lachlan, it was named by George Evans after Governor Lachlan Macquarie, in 1813.
The Macquarie Marshes are protected as a wetland of international importance.

q.q: What forms where the Macquarie spreads out on the plains?

Q79082.t: The Volga's great partner, winding through taiga
Q79082.s: Deep taiga surrounds the upper Kama, which loops in a huge arc north before turning south towards Perm. By the time it meets the Volga below Kazan it carries so much water that, by some measures, it could count as the main river rather than the tributary. It is the Volga's largest tributary, about 1,800 km long.
Q79082.w: Dark, unbroken taiga, with pale sandbars and oxbow lakes on the river's bends.
f: The Kama rises from springs near the village of Kuliga in Udmurtia.
Further down, dams turn it into a chain of huge reservoirs, among them the Kama and Votkinsk seas.
Perm, the largest city on the Kama, grew up around an 18th-century copper works.

q.q: Which river does the Kama flow into?

Q843308.t: One of Africa's deepest canyons, below the Simien
Q843308.s: The Tekezé has cut one of the deepest canyons in Africa, winding through the Ethiopian highlands in a gorge up to about 2,000 m deep. Here it curves around the eastern side of the Simien Mountains, whose highest peak, Ras Dashen, rises above 4,500 m. Further on it becomes the Setit, joins the Atbara and finally reaches the Nile.
Q843308.w: A thin river deep in a vast, branching canyon, with high green-brown plateaus and jagged peaks to the west.
f: The Tekezé Dam, finished in 2009, was among the tallest arch dams in Africa when it was built.
The Simien Mountains beside it are a UNESCO World Heritage site, home to gelada monkeys.
In the rainy season it swells into a roaring torrent; in the dry season it shrinks to a thread.

q.q: Which great river does the Tekezé's water finally reach?

Q216941.t: The Pearl River's great trunk, squeezing through gorges
Q216941.s: Near Zhaoqing the Xi, the main stem of the Pearl River, squeezes through short gorges between green hills before spreading into the vast Pearl River Delta. Beyond, the land becomes a web of channels, fish ponds and some of the largest cities on Earth. Zhaoqing itself sits beside a lake studded with the limestone peaks of the Seven Star Crags.
Q216941.w: A broad brown river leaving green hills through a narrow gap, then fanning out into a flat delta of channels and cities.
f: Matteo Ricci lived in Zhaoqing in the 1580s and drew his first Chinese map of the world there.
The Xi is about 2,200 km long, the longest branch of the Pearl River system.
The Pearl River system carries more water than any Chinese river except the Yangtze.

q.q: Which river system is the Xi the main stem of?

Q127892.t: Lake-wide between two cities and two countries
Q127892.s: Posadas in Argentina and Encarnación in Paraguay face each other across the Paraná here, joined by a long bridge. Downstream the Yacyretá dam has raised the water, so the river is broad and lake-like. Nearby stand the ruins of Jesuit missions, where Guaraní communities lived in planned towns in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Q127892.w: A very wide, calm river between two facing cities, with a long bridge and red-earth fields on both banks.
f: At about 4,900 km, the Paraná is the second-longest river in South America.
The Jesuit missions of Trinidad, Jesús and San Ignacio Miní are UNESCO World Heritage sites.
Yacyretá dam is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in South America.

q.q: Which two cities face each other across the Paraná here?

Q643.t: Italy's longest river, slow across a fog-bound plain
Q643.s: Italy's longest river crosses the flat, intensely farmed Po Valley in broad, lazy loops, lined with poplar plantations and sandbars. In winter the valley often lies under thick fog, and only the Alps and Apennines poke through. Here it flows between Piacenza and Cremona, the city where Antonio Stradivari made his violins.
Q643.w: A wide, looping river with pale sandbars and rows of poplars, crossing a flat, geometric plain of fields.
f: The Po runs about 650 km from Monte Viso in the Alps to its delta on the Adriatic.
Cremona's violin-making tradition is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
Fed by the river's silt, its delta is still growing into the Adriatic.

q.q: Which famous violin maker worked in Cremona, near the Po?

Q1469.s: Châteaux line the banks of the Loire, and its wide, shallow bed is scattered with pale sandbanks and wooded islands. Here between Amboise and Chaumont, the valley is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. At about 1,000 km, the Loire is France's longest river, and one of the least tamed in western Europe.
Q1469.w: A wide, shallow river braided with pale sandbanks and green islands, running west through a gentle valley of fields and woods.
f: Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years at Amboise and died there in 1519.
The Loire Valley between Sully-sur-Loire and Chalonnes has been a UNESCO site since 2000.
The Loire rises on Mont Gerbier de Jonc in the Massif Central.

q.q: Which artist spent his last years at Amboise on the Loire?
